title: Pride Before a Fall in Judah
overview: Judah's King Amaziah wins a battle, grows proud, picks a disastrous fight with Israel, and dies in a plot, while Israel's wrongdoing King Jeroboam II is still allowed to win back lost land.

parts.label: Amaziah's mixed start (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Amaziah is called good but not wholehearted, and the local hilltop shrines, places of worship outside the Jerusalem temple, stayed in use. He executed the men who murdered his father but spared their children, following Moses' law; in the ancient world it was common to wipe out a traitor's whole family.

parts.label: Victory over Edom (v. 7)
parts.note: Edom, a neighbouring people to the southeast, had broken free from Judah a generation earlier, and Amaziah fought to bring it back under control. Sela means "the rock" and is often linked with the later city of Petra, though scholars are not certain.

parts.label: The thistle and the cedar (vv. 8-14)
parts.note: Fresh from that win, Amaziah challenged Israel's King Jehoash, who answered with a mocking fable: a weed asking a mighty cedar for a marriage alliance, then getting trampled. Amaziah would not back down, and Judah was crushed: Jerusalem's wall was broken open for about 600 feet, and the temple and palace treasures were carried off along with hostages.

parts.label: Three kings' endings (vv. 15-22)
parts.note: Jehoash dies, and Amaziah outlives him by fifteen years but is hunted down and killed by conspirators at Lachish, a fortified town in Judah. The text does not say why, though his ruinous war likely cost him support; his sixteen year old son Azariah, also called Uzziah, takes over and rebuilds the Red Sea port of Elath.

parts.label: Jeroboam II's surprising success (vv. 23-29)
parts.note: Jeroboam II kept the worship at the golden calf shrines that the first Jeroboam had set up long before, yet he restored Israel's old borders, as the prophet Jonah (the same Jonah of the later book) had foretold. The writer says this happened because the LORD saw how bitterly the people were suffering, not because the king earned it; the remark about Damascus and Hamath "belonging to Judah" is unclear in the original language, and scholars are unsure what it means.

think: Why do you think a win in one area of life can make people feel ready to take on far more than they can handle?
